findings.rationale: The packet and retrieved passages do not establish the cause of this accident, so the cause is not determined from the available evidence.

The packet notes the pilot had not completed a flight review in decades and had a denied medical in 2009, suggesting currency and qualification concerns, similar to the precedent's pilot-experience context.

The retrieved experimental-aircraft precedent notes a pilot's prior accident and limited recorded experience, but the packet itself gives little direct evidence of planning or preparation failures for this incident.

The engine failed to produce power after a return to airport; the right magneto not producing spark and the engine's long idle/age point to an engine power-plant failure, with the precedent showing partial power loss attributed to engine-related causes that could not be determined.
The right magneto would not produce spark when rotated by hand, indicating an ignition system malfunction as a probable cause of the engine's inability to restart and deliver power.

The pilot's use of the wrong-length bolts after an engine conversion shows maintenance task errors causing in-flight power loss, a comparable maintenance-related mechanism, though the present record lacks direct evidence of an error.

The pilot's decision to fly an unfamiliar, recently purchased airplane with stale fuel and no recent flights shows planning and preparation shortfalls, though the precedents involve different accident mechanisms.

The packet indicates VMC with 10 sm visibility and a snow-covered runway, so weather-related conditions are a possible but unsupported contributor; the cited precedent involves a downdraft rather than visibility, so the link is weak.

The packet describes left brake assembly degradation (angular pad wear, corroded and pitted anchor bolts) that produced asymmetric drag and a leftward ground track, and the cited passage similarly involves a landing gear component failure during takeoff roll that caused a directional and collapse event.
The runway surface condition (icy runway) contributed to the disabled airplane leaving the runway, and the passage's runway-related factual context is only loosely analogous, so this is a weak fit.
Weather conditions were VMC with 10 sm visibility, so ceiling/visibility is unlikely to be a cause; the cited passage does not establish a comparable visibility-related mechanism.

The crew's decision to continue an unstabilized approach with excessive descent rate and tailwind, rather than executing a missed approach, reflects an information processing or decision failure similar to the approach-path failure in the precedent.

Gusting tailwind of about 15 knots on a wet runway contributed to the excessive landing speed and hydroplaning, though the precedent passage itself concerns a tailwheel lock rather than wind, so support here is weak.
The captain's abrupt power chop and rapid descent to land are control actions that deviated from the approach path, paralleling the precedent's failure to maintain an adequate approach path.

The engine's compressor bleed-off valve malfunction (slow closure, air leakage) is an engine control/bleed component failure, but the retrieved passage about landing gear bolts does not actually support this; a weak match, so treated cautiously.
The compressor bleed-off valve is part of the engine bleed air system and its slow closure and leakage caused the observed engine anomalies during test-run.
Examination found power section buckling and internal rotational contact of the exhaust casing in the turbine section, a turbine engine internal failure that preceded the accident.
The BOV was repaired by an overhaul facility in 2012 and the part was not installed at delivery, with non-standard part-number marking, suggesting a maintenance task performance issue.

The engine lost power in cruise with no mechanism confirmed; the packet's carburetor icing conditions point to an engine fuel and control problem, similar to the precedent engine power loss accidents.
The pilot did not use carburetor heat during troubleshooting and then made a high, fast approach and a long landing, reflecting info processing and decision errors.
Temperature and dew point at the nearby station were conducive to serious carburetor icing at cruise power, which is an environmental condition that could explain the rough running.
The student pilot's diagnosis and approach decisions under an engine emergency reflect task prioritization and workload management issues.

The incident involved an engine that would not accelerate past 45% Ng due to a fractured FCU control lever arm, a fuel control component failure; the retrieved passage about a helicopter power loss sequence offers only loose support for an engine fuel-control mechanism, so confidence is moderate.
Engine power loss with rotor rpm decay mirrors the reported loss of engine power, but the passage does not establish an engine-level cause for this incident.

The instructor and pilot receiving instruction appear to have made poor decisions in a multi-engine airplane they were not current in, and the unusual erratic flight and spiral suggest inadequate information processing or decision-making, similar to the inadequate-correction and controlled-flight-into-terrain precedents.

The pilot receiving instruction had only about 9 multi-engine hours and no time in the accident make and model, indicating a training/qualification gap relevant to the loss of control during the flight.

Toxicology showed alprazolam, zolpidem, and citalopram in the flight instructor, which the FAA considers impairing, so impairment of mental state is a plausible contributor, though it is not confirmed as causal here.
Medical history of the flight instructor includes medication use and prior impairment, but no retrieved passage directly supports a physical health finding for this incident, so confidence is low.

The pilot continued a descent and did not respond to repeated controller calls and low altitude alerts, suggesting a decision/information processing failure, though the cited passage addresses a different stall mechanism and is only loosely analogous.

Forecast and PIREP icing conditions with supercooled large droplets and freezing temperatures indicate an icing environment that is the likely environmental factor, though no icing precedent passage is cited directly.

The pilot's failure to respond to ATC alerts over about 10 minutes of descent points to an attention/monitoring lapse, supported by the general pattern that inadequate monitoring led to loss of control in the precedent.
The pilot lacked documented recent instrument proficiency for IMC flight, a qualification deficiency relevant to this IMC icing accident.
Night IMC with mist and a 300 ft broken ceiling at the time of the accident is a visibility and ceiling condition that may have contributed to spatial disorientation or loss of control over water.

Pilot decision-making or fuel management error could be a factor in a fatal loss-of-control or power-loss accident, but the packet does not establish the cause; this precedent involves fuel mismanagement, which is only weakly similar here.
Night, low-visibility conditions over water raise the possibility of perception or orientation problems, though no pilot-error evidence is present in the packet.

The packet's engine power loss traced to a water-contaminated fuel regulator reference line in the throttle body injector points to engine fuel and control malfunction, but the cited passage is only weakly analogous, so confidence is moderate.
Weather was VMC with no icing or temperature-related evidence in the packet, so this is a weak candidate for the water intrusion mechanism and is low confidence.
The pilot's delayed or poor action during a takeoff/ground roll led to a runway excursion in the precedent, a loose parallel to the veer-right and loss of control here.

Ground roll with braking issues and a runway excursion is discussed in the precedent, but the precedent's braking problem was in the brake system, not the landing gear, so support for this label is weak.
The precedent's runway excursion involved surface conditions, and the current accident ended in deep gravel adjacent to the runway, though the passage does not directly describe gravel.
The engine suffered connecting rod separation from the crankshaft causing loss of power, a similar engine internal failure leading to power loss in the precedent accident.
Failure to perform required valve/camshaft inspection and service bulletin compliance parallels the precedent's maintenance task performance issues where engine work was not properly completed.

The precedent involved maintenance-related engine failure, but the packet's maintenance record gaps (no 400-hour or camshaft lobe inspection) are not clearly supported by the cited passage for an organizational training finding.

The incident involves a landing gear system malfunction (gear would not properly extend and mechanical emergency extension was resisted), and the retrieved passage documents a landing gear collapse-related accident with gear system damage.

The packet reports inaccurate fuel gauge readings with an empty left tank, which points to a fuel system indication issue, but the cited passage is only loosely analogous and does not directly address fuel quantity indication.

The pilot's prolonged 40-minute circling while diagnosing the gear problem suggests a use-of-equipment or information issue, and the cited probable cause involves a false indication leading to a precautionary shutdown.
Engine fire originated in the No. 2 engine nacelle area, but none of the retrieved passages describe an engine-internal failure leading to this fire, so the link is only speculative.

The packet reports no mechanical malfunction found in postaccident testing and no data anomaly explaining the dual power loss, so the cause is undetermined on the available evidence.

The packet notes fuel-stained crossover tube connections and modified induction plumbing on both engines, pointing toward an engine fuel/induction delivery problem, which the passage's engine-control discussion loosely parallels.

Simultaneous loss of power to both engines is the central event here, and the precedent passage describes engine power-management issues on a twin-engine aircraft, though it does not establish an engine cause for this accident.

The pilot's decisions during the departure (rushed start attempts, flooding, departing before engine warmed, and continuing climb after engine loss) reflect information processing and decision errors, and the retrieved takeoff-failure passages show similar takeoff loss-of-control precedent.

The pilot did not allow the engine to warm and did not perform a run-up, reflecting inadequate pre-takeoff task preparation, though the cited passage only loosely matches as a precedent for pre-departure procedure.

Loss of engine power after takeoff is central here, and the fuel-delivery investigation in the cited passage illustrates how fuel system restriction can cause power loss, though no engine fault was established for this incident.

The engine internal failure with oil loss and thermal damage in the packet is a powerplant engine mechanical failure, and the retrieved factual passage documents engine examination of a failed Cessna-type piston engine, which supports coding the engine component failure.

The 34-year gap since last overhaul and cylinder replacements suggest an inadequate maintenance or inspection task, and the retrieved probable cause shows an inadequate preflight inspection leading to an engine power loss.
The packet's oil accumulation and loss of oil quantity relate to fluid condition, and the retrieved passage shows oil system examination as part of a powerplant fluids analysis.

Night, dark, unlit terrain with limited visual cues (the right-seat pilot reported he could not see anything) is a ceiling/visibility/light-condition related environmental factor; the cited passage describes a mountainous-terrain accident in similar limited-visibility conditions, though its causes differ.
The accident occurred at night over an unlit wetland with a 96% illuminated moon, making light condition a plausible contributing environmental factor.

Descent into dark terrain while relying on the flight's instruments suggests spatial disorientation (somatogravic illusion described in the packet); the cited passage shows an encounter with an environmental hazard leading to loss of control, which is only loosely analogous.

Continuing VFR flight into dark conditions over unlit terrain and a rapid uncontrolled descent point to poor in-flight decision-making, as the cited probable cause attributes an accident to poor decision-making.

The incident involved a cockpit door/hatch separating in flight causing structural damage and loss of control, a fuselage-structure failure; the retrieved passages do not directly describe a door separation, so the structural label is only weakly supported.

Flight control cable separations and aileron/elevator/trim damage in the packet point to a flight control system involvement, with the Beech 400 passage illustrating a system anomaly leading to damage, though the cause is not established.
The pilot's unusual attitude and erratic flight after the door loss suggests a possible information processing or decision issue, but the packet does not establish the pilot's response as causal.

The fuel pump voltage spikes and reduced fuel flow point to an engine fuel and control problem, though the cited passage concerns fuel exhaustion rather than fuel control malfunction.
The fuel system was implicated through the fuel pump and fuel supply restriction, consistent with a fuel system finding, though the cited precedent is a fuel exhaustion case.
Weak support only; the retrieved passages do not describe debris or foreign object effects on fuel systems, so this label is not well supported.
Strong, gusting crosswind conditions were a central environmental factor in the loss of directional control after touchdown, as in the prior crosswind-landing accident.
The crew continued an approach with a crosswind and gusts exceeding limits, a decision-making lapse analogous to the prior crosswind landing and pilot-decision cases.
Crew workload and wind-check procedures were stressed during the approach, and the pilot continued despite wind information that was incompletely checked.
Schedule and passenger-transport pressure discussed by the crew may have biased the go-around and continue decision, though the passage only loosely supports this.
No retrieved passage supports a planning or preparation finding; the passages are unrelated to this pilot's preparation.

The pilot's flight into a tower and fatal outcome, combined with the packet's drug-impairment evidence (delta-8-THC, gabapentin), suggests impaired decision making; the cited passage notes information processing/decision errors in a similar in-flight encounter, though its facts differ.

The pilot's failure to notice and avoid the tower with a low-altitude flight suggests an attention/monitoring lapse, which the cited analysis of a flight-path deviation that went unrecognized by the crew loosely parallels.

The airplane struck a manmade obstacle (a 197-ft MET tower) that was not charted, and the cited passage describes an airplane impacting an obstacle (seawall) in a deviation scenario, supporting object/obstacle as an environmental factor.

Gabapentin and delta-8-THC in the pilot's system could have caused impairment, and the cited probable cause of a failure to maintain adequate glidepath that led to an obstacle impact is a similar outcome, though it does not mention impairment.

The fuel selector valve was misrigged 180 degrees, so the selector positions did not correspond to the tanks supplying fuel, a fuel-system malfunction analogous to fuel selector mismanagement in the cited accident.
The pilot misjudged the fuel selector state and misdiagnosed the fuel supply situation, an information processing and decision error similar to the cited accident.
The pilot's failure to verify the fuel selector and tank status during preflight and run-up is a task performance issue consistent with the cited fuel management failure.

Toxicology showed sertraline (an antidepressant with possible cognitive effects) and a major-depression context, and the precedent links impairing medical conditions and medications to a fatal pilot-error accident, though the packet does not establish impairment.
The packet and retrieved passages do not establish the causal sequence after the ADS-B track ended during the turn, so the cause may remain undetermined.
Weather was VMC with 10 sm visibility, so no supporting precedent passage justifies a weather-related finding.

The loose ground feed-through stud in the electrical system caused the loss of electrical and engine power, mapping to electrical power system; the passage is only loosely analogous (gear fluid service) so it offers weak support, and the citation primarily reflects a maintenance-induced system failure pattern.

The improperly secured ground connection, lacking lock washer and locknut, reflects a maintenance/inspection lapse, and the precedent shows an underserviced condition leading to failure on an experimental-style airframe.

Model sounding shows temperatures near freezing with dewpoint spreads favoring serious carburetor icing at the altitudes flown, but the cited passage is only weakly connected and does not itself establish icing as cause here.
Cause is largely undetermined because the pilot and passenger had limited recollection and no clear mechanical failure was found, though no retrieved passage directly supports this label.

The pilot's decision to proceed without checking proper maintenance data and the poor preflight/maintenance judgment closely parallels the pilot's inadequate information processing and decision-making in the precedent accident involving improper propeller reinstallation without proper technical data.
Water and debris were found in the fuel of both carburetors and fuel boost pump samples, indicating a fuel system contamination mechanism that could cause the loss of power after takeoff.

The pilot did not perform a complete preflight inspection or fuel sampling, and the airplane was released after a week of repairs and rain exposure, reflecting inadequate task planning and preparation.
Contaminated fuel reaching the carburetors would disrupt engine fuel delivery, consistent with the power loss and sputtering after takeoff described in the narrative.
Environmental wind conditions at the time were light, so weather is a weak contributing factor, and the precedent only tangentially relates to a wind-related event.

The engine lost power and ran rough in cruise, and the teardown found no fault in the timing or ignition, but the passage shows a power loss from a mechanical engine failure, which is the closest precedent for an internal engine problem.
The packet does not identify the specific cause of the rough running, so the engine-related cause is not determined from the evidence available.

The rough running and hesitation in a carbureted engine with fuel-related symptoms in the precedent suggest a possible fuel delivery or control problem, though the packet notes normal fuel flow and pressure until 1042.

The pilot's in-flight decisions during an emergency (loss of engine power/fire, navigation to an unfamiliar airport at night) suggest an information processing or decision-making issue, though the retrieved precedents are only loosely analogous.

The engine lost power in flight with evidence of a fuel-supply problem (loose metered fuel hose b-nut at the metering valve outlet), and precedents show engine power loss from fuel or induction issues.
The pilot had never been to Clearwater and was unfamiliar with the airport, and precedents cite pilot actions leading to loss of control, supporting a possible experience/qualification factor.

The pilot operated with main wing tanks deliberately empty for aerobatic center-of-gravity reasons and then flew a takeoff with fuel exhaustion risk, a decision-making lapse; the cited passages show pilot decision-related findings in similar mechanical-normal accidents.
Inadequate flight planning and fuel management resembles the planning-related probable cause in the cited precedent, supporting a use-of-equipment/information or planning concern.
Weather was benign (VMC, 7 kt wind), so no weather-related finding is supported; included only as a low-confidence placeholder is not justified and is left out.
The fuel selector found in OFF rather than the intended tank, with the cause of the fuel starvation tied to a crew action on the selector, parallels the selector-position error in this incident.
Improper use of the fuel selector equipment led to fuel flow loss, similar to the selector not being fully seated in the detent in this accident.
Engine loss of power from fuel exhaustion during approach is a fuel system related power loss, relevant as precedent for fuel-supply-related loss of engine power.

Engine rough running, rpm loss, and metallic debris including bearing and piston ring fragments point to an internal engine (power plant) failure, though the cited passage is only a weakly related precedent.
A prior engine vibration and power problem in a similar airplane led to a powerplant-level finding, supporting a general power plant failure classification here.
The precise underlying engine failure mechanism is not fully established in the packet, so an undetermined finding may be appropriate alongside the powerplant codes.

The crew's decision to perform a stall test in icing-related conditions with marginal weather and an airspeed deceleration led to a loss of control, similar to crew decision errors in the precedents cited.
The crew's stall-recovery and stall-test proficiency appears inadequate (training did not include full stalls and the SIC had limited stall-prevention experience), which is a training/knowledge gap.

Icing exposure from precipitation and sleet after the wing leading edges were removed reduced maximum lift and stall angle, consistent with an environmental icing contribution to the aileron-snatch roll upset.

The retrieved passage is a reciprocating engine accident where no pre-mishap mechanical malfunction was found, so it offers limited precedent for an engine-internal failure finding here.

The landing gear system failed to remain in a usable configuration, and the retrieved passage documents a landing gear structural failure leading to accident damage, supporting a landing gear system finding.

Gear-up landing after a pilot action sequence resembles pilot action-level errors where the pilot's handling of the airplane led to damage, though the passage is a taxi incident rather than a gear-up landing.

The helicopter's erratic altitude, airspeed and heading changes after entering IMC are consistent with spatial disorientation from loss of outside visual references, as explained in the cited passage on vestibular illusions in the absence of visual cues.

The pilot continued a VFR night flight into deteriorating conditions and deviated from the planned course, reflecting a decision to proceed despite weather and an inoperative radar altimeter, consistent with the cited discussion of get-there-itis and decision-making.

The radar altimeter was inoperative and intermittently failing before the flight, which degraded a navigation/altitude-awareness system; the cited passage is only loosely related, so confidence is moderate.

Night IMC conditions with low ceilings and reduced visibility over mountainous desert terrain contributed to the loss of visual references, though the cited passage addresses the mechanism rather than this weather specifically.

The pilot departed with a known unresolved airworthiness/equipment problem after a brief troubleshooting attempt, suggesting inadequate preflight planning and maintenance-discrepancy handling, as in the cited precedent of continued flight after known control problems.

The pilot's decision to continue with a high, fast approach and push the nose down, followed by inability to control the landing, parallels precedent where pilot action during landing led to a runway excursion.
The pilot's failure to manage the approach energy and stabilize the approach before landing is a planning/execution issue comparable to the directional control failure in the precedent accident.
A 7-knot tailwind on a displaced-threshold runway reduced available landing distance and contributed to the overrun, though the precedent itself does not establish wind as a cause.
The packet describes damage and post-accident findings but does not identify a causal factor, so the cause is not determined from the available evidence.

The airplane struck a tree during the accident sequence, an object-collision scenario analogous to the cited inflight collision with an object, though the packet does not establish the cause of the event.

The retrieved passage describes ATC failing to provide required weather information to a pilot avoiding weather, a situation analogous to the unrelayed PIREP and weather-avoidance decisions in this incident.

The airplane struck powerlines spanning the river, an object/obstacle hazard in the physical environment, and the passage shows that object contact by aircraft is a relevant causal category for an accident of this type.

The engine showed no obvious mechanical issue and the cause of the powerline strike was not clearly determined, so a not-determined finding is supported by precedent where causes could not be established.

The low-level flight at high rpm near powerlines suggests a decision/information processing issue in the pilot's low-altitude flight planning, paralleling the improper low-altitude decision in the cited probable cause.

The alternator rotating magnet slipped on its shaft, an electrical power system component failure, and the cited passage similarly documents a loss of engine power traced to a loose fitting, showing that mechanical looseness can cause power loss.

The accident involved a modified automotive engine, and the cited passage describes an engine power-related investigation of similar engine-related analysis, though the link to this accident's ignition/alternator findings is weak.

Maintenance task performance is supported by the packet's finding that a B-nut lacked thread engagement after an inspection that required torque paint verification, though the cited passage itself does not discuss maintenance.

Engine power loss with the fuel control system and engine controls found in normal condition is a precedent for a power-control-related loss of power, though the precedent is a generic total loss of power.
The precedent involves a total loss of engine power with no mechanical anomalies found, which is only loosely analogous to this fuel control pressure line failure.

Non-instrument-rated pilot flying into IMC with sustained turns is the precedent for spatial disorientation, which matches the low, circling post-takeoff flight in snow and the inadequate instrument experience here.
Continuing VFR flight into instrument conditions despite a weather briefing indicating IMC reflects an information processing and decision error, as in the precedent.
Heavy snow reducing visibility to about 1/2 mile and creating IMC conditions at departure is an environmental ceiling and visibility factor.

Toxicology showing impairing drug use in the pilot is precedent for an impairment finding, though the passages here only tie that to a different case and the diphenhydramine evidence is postmortem and uncertain.

The packet describes an elevator control cable separating in flight, and the retrieved analysis describes a control linkage disconnecting from its connection, which is an analogous flight-control-type failure mechanism, though it concerns an engine control rather than the elevator system.

The cable was replaced in January 2023 and the failure followed about 316 hours later, so a maintenance task performance deficiency is plausible, and the retrieved passage shows a similar pattern of an unsecured retaining bolt with no safety wire and missing secondary retention.
Loss of engine power in a Rotax 582 powered homebuilt aircraft after a short flight is a closely analogous precedent, though the cited passage concerns a different engine failure mechanism.
Missing storage-preservation maintenance entries suggest a records and maintenance oversight issue, but no retrieved passage supports this label directly.

The pilot had only 9 hours in the make and model, no Cessna 182 logbook entries, and a loosely recent flying history, which parallels the earlier accident where a pilot flying seldom in an unfamiliar airplane lacked currency.

The pilot's repeated unstabilized, uncoordinated approaches and loss of directional control after a left yaw resemble the earlier probable cause of loss of directional control, though the earlier accident involved a stall at takeoff.

The packet's evidence of valve guide deposits and valve stem clearance problems points to an engine-internal valve train degradation, though none of the retrieved passages directly describe this mechanism.
The absence of maintenance on cylinders and valves over 646 hours, combined with the sludge buildup, suggests a maintenance-related task performance issue, but no retrieved passage supports this.

Operating procedures such as leaning and avoiding long ground operation were not followed in a manner that the packet implies, pointing to a decision/information processing issue, but no retrieved passage supports it.

The pilot's decisions during the approach, including continuing a low approach and attempting a short-field landing with the instructor, resemble poor information processing and decision-making in precedent accidents involving adverse decisions in marginal conditions.
The use of a view-limiting device during the instrument approach and the unknown fuel quantity relate to task performance and use of equipment, though passages support this only weakly.
The tower's runway switching and the shifting 11-knot wind may have contributed to the unstable approach, but the passages only weakly support wind-related causation here.

The pilot in a low-altitude turn-to-final accident with a gust encounter and an apparent late recovery suggests an information processing or decision issue during the approach, which the precedent passage illustrates with a similar base-to-final loss of altitude.

Gusting wind at the airport (10 kt gusting 16 kt with a shifting direction) during the final turn is a plausible environmental contributor, paralleled by the precedent gust-induced altitude loss on final.
Management of flaps and power on a short final may be a workload issue, but no retrieved passage directly supports it for this incident.

The helicopter's overrunning clutch output bearing was not removed and repacked during the 300-hour grease task, and a maintenance-task error causing a component to separate in flight is a similar maintenance-inspection failure to the cited precedent.

Mechanics did not perform the output bearing removal and repack as the maintenance manual required, and the cited precedent attributes an in-flight separation to an incorrect maintenance latching, which is the same kind of personnel maintenance-task failure.
The packet shows a fuel leak and a loose fuel line at the throttle body preventing normal engine fuel delivery, and the precedent passage links fuel delivery failure to a loss of engine power.
The fuel system delivery path to the engine was disrupted by a leak at the throttle body line, which the precedent associates with engine power loss from fuel supply problems.
The pilot's continued flight at 2,500 ft, overflight, and failure to execute a timely landing reflect decision/information processing issues, though the passage only loosely parallels this case.
The pilot's low night and limited recent experience may have contributed to workload management problems on a night approach, though the packet's link is indirect.
The packet does not establish a definitive cause; the engine damage, GPS data loss, and flight profile are not explained by the retrieved passages.

The steep unrecoverable descent into a hill with no evident mechanical cause could reflect spatial disorientation or loss of control, as in the cited accident, though the packet does not establish the pilot's state.
Continued flight toward a destination and a steep descent into terrain may reflect an information processing or decision error, a pattern described in the cited analysis.

The crankshaft fatigue cracking in the engine is an engine-internal failure, and the cited probable cause involves partial loss of power from an engine-related condition, which is the closest precedent for an engine component failure.
The power plant as a whole was the source of the loss of power, and the cited precedent describes a power loss attributed to an undetermined powerplant-related condition.

The incident's primary cause lies in maintenance-related degradation (corroded and worn aileron cables, corroded pulley) that a required inspection should have detected, and the retrieved passage shows a maintenance-related cause in a prior flight-control accident.
The aileron direct cable separation caused loss of aileron control, which is a flight control system failure, though the retrieved passage only shows a generic flight control issue.

The packet describes a pilot with a documented mental health condition and sedating medications, and the closest precedent involves a pilot attributing a loss of control to slow reaction time, which supports mental/emotional state or impairment as relevant to the aircraft control loss.

The airplane stalled during a low-altitude turn, similar to the precedent where a low, slow pilot was too late to respond to a stall, pointing to a decision/information processing error in maintaining airspeed and angle of attack.

The toxicology showing gabapentin, venlafaxine and diphenhydramine suggests possible drug-related impairment of the pilot's performance during the turn, and the precedent links pilot control failure to impairment-type causes.
The pilot's low-altitude steep turn after takeoff likely caused an inadvertent stall, which in the precedent was attributed to the pilot's late action in response to the stall.

The crew's decision-making in continuing with a high-speed landing roll and disabling autobrakes on a reported slippery runway is an information processing/decision error, and the precedent cited shows a pilot-directional-control failure stemming from crew action.

The captain's manual deceleration and disarming of autobrakes/speedbrakes was an action error in a landing context, analogous to the precedent where a pilot's inadvertent control action caused the accident.
The IMC approach with low ceilings and reduced visibility is a relevant environmental condition, though the precedent only supports that such conditions were present rather than causal.
The precedent of an excessive approach speed leading to a hard landing parallels the high groundspeed touchdown and workload-driven deceleration management in this event.

Carburetor icing conditions (80°F and 71°F dew point) are an environmental condition, but the passages provided do not directly address icing weather; the closest precedent involves carburetor-equipped Cessna engine examination without icing findings, so this label is weakly supported.

The pilot did not use carburetor heat, a use-of-equipment failure, and the precedent passage documents carburetor heat and mixture control positions being examined as part of the cockpit control review.

Icing conditions with supercooled large droplets forecast and present in the area suggest a possible environmental contribution, but the passages provided do not directly support an icing-based finding.

None of the retrieved passages address retardant-induced corrosion or comingling, so the cause cannot be determined from precedent, and the packet's own corrosion evidence is unassigned to any taxonomy code supported by these passages.
The retrieved passage concerns an in-flight fire from an unapproved fuel line, which is only loosely analogous to the structural corrosion found on the airtanker fuselage and tank structure.

The crew's failure to verify the altimeter setting, brief the approach, and appropriately respond to deviations is an information processing/decision error, and the retrieved probable causes show similar pilot decision-based accidents tied to incomplete information review.

The PIC's documented struggles with FMS, approach minimums, and incomplete training on the accident type suggest a training-related deficiency, though the retrieved precedent is only loosely analogous.

Improper use of flight management and autoflight information (FLOC mode confusion, autopilot state, altimeter setting) is consistent with a use-of-equipment/information error, supported only weakly by the precedent.

The pilot admitted drinking before the flight, toxicology relevant to impairment was reported, and the NTSB narrative describes an impaired pilot who continued the flight, but none of the retrieved passages discusses alcohol impairment as a cause, so this rests on the packet alone.

The pilot continued the flight into deteriorating weather, repeatedly descended below clouds at night, and attempted to divert, which points to an information processing or decision error, though no retrieved precedent describes a similar decision.

Rain and a descending ceiling at night, with reported TWT ceilings of 700 ft broken and 1,300 ft overcast, were environmental conditions the pilot could not safely fly in VFR, but no retrieved passage addresses ceiling or visibility as a cause.
Engine power loss after fuel delivery was impeded, with water and fuel system contamination found in the fuel flow path, parallels a fuel-starvation style engine fuel system failure.

Foreign substance (water) contaminating the fuel path, as with debris blocking the fuel outlet in the precedent, could be a physical-environment/substance cause, though the packet does not establish the source.

The packet describes a total loss of electrical power after generator/starter switch misconfiguration and a depleted battery, and the passage concerns a system-related failure with an unverified precedent.
Retrieved passage is about a different accident; the relevant precedent is weak here, so this label is only loosely supported by the packet's electrical-failure decision-making and is uncertain.

The incident involves a landing gear retraction failure with the left main gear retracted and a broken retract rod, which is a landing gear system malfunction; the cited passage describes a gear separation/bent gear in a prior accident but only weakly parallels the mechanism.

Retract rod punctured the gearbox case, but no retrieved passage directly supports a nacelle structure finding, so this is speculative and omitted from high confidence.

The pilot's sudden control inputs on approach (here, the pilot taking control and the aircraft turning and drifting with fast approach speed) resemble the unexplained sudden right turn on approach in the precedent, suggesting a decision/information processing issue, though the packet does not establish the cause.

The pilot's logbook shows no flights since 2015 and no flight instructor rating, and the fast approach and loss of control during instruction suggest inadequate recent experience, which is a plausible contributing factor in the precedent of pilot-caused accidents.
No aircraft maintenance records or logbooks were available, so maintenance status could not be verified, but the packet does not show a maintenance-caused failure, so this is only a weak possibility.
Rain and reduced visibility (1 3/4 sm, broken ceiling at 800 ft) reported at the time of the accident are a meteorological factor comparable to the low visibility in the cited fog accident.

The pilot continued a landing approach into deteriorating IMC and gusty weather after being warned of precipitation, a decision-making problem that resembles the fog-related loss of control in the cited accident.
